entries.modern_form: PIE *ger- 'to turn, wind; curving, crooked' (Pokorny 3. ger- 385-390; Watkins/AHD ger-² 'curving, crooked')
entries.note: The root box is right on all three counts. Pokorny's lemma reads 'Root / lemma: ger-3 / Meaning: to turn, wind' with 'Page(s): 385-390', so Nourai's POK:385 is the first page of exactly that article; Watkins's appendix has 'ger-2. Curving, crooked; hypothetical Indo-European base for a variety of Germanic words with initial kr- ... [Pok. 3. ger- 385.]' and organises the material in two halves, 'I. Words meaning to bend, curl; bent, crooked, hooked' and 'II. Words meaning a rounded mass, collection; a round object, vessel, container' — which is where Nourai's three-part gloss 'crooked, curved, round object' comes from. ('Ger 1' is Nourai's own numbering, not Pokorny's; Pokorny's ger-1 is 'to gather', ger-2 'to cry hoarsely', ger-4 'to grow up'.) Every Germanic/Romance box of the chart is one of Watkins's numbered items, and the Indo-Iranian branch is Pokorny's own dental extension. Three things need correcting, all of them in the printed book rather than in the extraction (the JSON reproduces page 143 faithfully — checked against the page image, saved as data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/173.png). (1) Node #6 'Italian grappo : assemblage' should be gruppo: Watkins reads 'Italian gruppo, an assemblage: GROUP', and Klein, Webster and Buck all give gruppo; Italian grappo exists but means 'bunch (of grapes)'. (2) Node #9 'Germanic grâppon' should be *krāppōn-: Watkins prints '*krāppōn-, a hook, especially one used in harvesting grapes', and a Germanic form of this root must begin with k- by Grimm's law. (3) Node #2's second word, 'gravatha', is Mo'in's Old Iranian *gravath va — the footnote on the very page Nourai cites (Borhān p.1803, note 4) reads 'ایرانی باستان *gravathva «نیبرگ ص ۸۴»', and it is labelled Old Iranian there, not Old Persian. Nourai's Iranian material is otherwise exactly Mo'in's: note 10 of the same page gives 'از پارسی باستان *gratha ، سانسکریت grath (بستن) «هوبشمان ص۹۳»'.
entries.note_fa: خود ریشه درست است: پوکورنی در صفحات ۳۸۵–۳۹۰ مادهٔ ger-3 را با معنای «پیچیدن، تابیدن» آورده و واتکینز در پیوست فرهنگ American Heritage همان را ger-2 «curving, crooked» می‌نامد و مادهٔ خود را به دو بخش «خمیده/قلاب‌مانند» و «تودهٔ گرد، ظرف» بخش می‌کند؛ پس معنای سه‌جزئی نورایی عیناً از همین جاست. شمارهٔ «Ger 1» از آنِ خود نورایی است نه پوکورنی. سه لغزش در نمودار هست و هر سه از خودِ کتاب است نه از خوانش اسکن: ۱) ایتالیایی grappo باید gruppo باشد؛ ۲) صورت ژرمنی grâppon باید *krāppōn- باشد، زیرا g هندواروپایی بر پایهٔ قانون گریم در ژرمنی به k بدل می‌شود؛ ۳) صورت gravatha در حاشیهٔ معین (برهان قاطع ص ۱۸۰۳ حاشیهٔ ۴) *gravathva است و «ایرانی باستان» خوانده شده، نه پارسی باستان. در کل، ادعای نورایی دربارهٔ خود ریشه درست است.

ref_check.note: POK_full.txt line 31336ff: 'Root / lemma: ger-3 / Meaning: to turn, wind' ... 'References: WP. I 593 ff., WH. 623, Trautmann 94 f., 97, 99 f. / Page(s): 385-390'. Page 385 is the first page of the article, so Nourai's POK:385 points at the right lemma; the gloss he gives ('crooked, curved, round object') is Watkins's rendering of it rather than Pokorny's German 'drehen, winden'.

consulted.note: the article supplies almost every box of the chart: 'Old Indic granth-, grathnami ... granthi-h m. ‚knot, joint, intumescence‘, grantha-h ‚knot‘' (dental extension, p.386); 'Old Norse kartr, Old English craet m. ‚cart‘'; 'Old English cribb ‚crib, manger‘'; 'ags. cradol m. ‚Wiege‘'; 'Old English cryppel cripple', 'Old English creopan to creep'; 'Old English crycc, nengl. crutch'; 'Middle High German krol(le), krulle ‚curl‘' (p.389).

'ger-2. Curving, crooked; hypothetical Indo-European base for a variety of Germanic words with initial kr-. I. Words meaning to bend, curl; bent, crooked, hooked ... II. Words meaning “a rounded mass, collection; a round object, vessel, container.” ... [Pok. 3. ger- 385.]' (AHD_watkins1985.txt line 492ff).

the parent article of Pokorny's; the dental-extension paragraph reads 'idg. *gr-et(h)-, nasaliert *grenth-: ags. cradol m. ‚Wiege“ (*kradula- ‚geflochtenes“), ahd. kratto ‚Korb“ ... ai. granth-, grathnami, fut. granthisyami ‚winden, knüpfen, einen Knoten binden“' (WLD_Bd1_1930_dli_70244_djvu.txt lines 37410-37421).

'Skt. granthi- : grath- ‚tie‘, this perh. : OE cradel ‚cradle‘, OHG kratto ‚basket‘, fr. an extension of *ger- in words based on the notion of ‚twist, wind‘. Walde-P. 1.593 ff. (595)' — the same root and the same hedge ('perh.'); and 13.192 'NE group (fr. Fr. groupe, fr. Ital. gruppo : groppo ‚knot‘)'.

Mann sets up an independent IE noun 'grondhos, á (gronth-) ‚mass, tuft, bunch‘ Skt. cf. granthah, ih ‚knot‘; Gk. grónthos ‚balled fist, punch‘; Cor. gron ‚mass, bunch‘' rather than deriving it from *ger-, i.e. he keeps the Indic word but not Pokorny's derivation of it.

nodes.derivation: The Sanskrit material is real: the verbal root granth-/grath- 'to tie (a knot), string together' (present grathnāti, future granthiṣyati), participle grathita- 'knotted', with the nouns granthi- m. 'knot, joint, swelling' and grantha- 'knot' (later 'composition, book' — a text being 'tied together'). Pokorny puts exactly these forms under ger-3 as its nasalised dental extension: '2. Dental extensions: a. gr-et(h)-... b. Nasalized: Old Indic granth-, grathnāmi ... granthi-h m. ‚knot, joint‘, grantha-h ‚knot‘', beside Old English cradol and Old High German kratto ‚basket‘ — material printed on p.386, the page Nourai cites. So the arrow root→Sanskrit is Pokorny's own, and Walde-Pokorny I 595 and Buck 9.192 say the same. It is only 'plausible' because the newest specialist treatments hedge: Cheung (2007: 123, s.v. *graθH) writes 'A convincing IE etymology for this (Ir.) root is wanting. The Germanic nominal forms, ? OHG kratto ‚basket‘, OE cradol, Engl. cradle, NHG Kranz ... often cited as cognates are unattractive: are they rather loanwords from a "substrate" source?', and Wiktionary calls the derivation from *gre(n)tH- < *ger- 'traditional' but 'not certain'. Nourai's gloss 'knot' belongs strictly to the noun grantha-/granthi-, not to the verbal root.
nodes.derivation_fa: ریشهٔ سنسکریت granth-/grath- «گره زدن، بستن» (حال grathnāti) و اسم‌های granthi- «گره، بند» و grantha- «گره» به‌راستی موجودند و پوکورنی در همان صفحهٔ ۳۸۶ که نورایی یاد کرده، آن‌ها را زیر ریشهٔ ger-3 و به صورت گسترش‌یافتهٔ دندانی با خیشومی‌شدگی (*gre-n-th-) آورده است؛ والده–پوکورنی (ج۱ ص ۵۹۵) و باک نیز همین را می‌گویند. اما چونگ (۲۰۰۷، ص ۱۲۳) تصریح می‌کند که ریشهٔ هندواروپایی قانع‌کننده‌ای برای این ریشه در دست نیست و همریشه‌های ژرمنی شاید وام‌واژهٔ زیرلایه باشند؛ از این‌رو ادعای نورایی با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

OHG kratto ‚basket”, OE cradol ... are unattractive: are they rather loanwords from a "substrate" source?'

nodes.derivation: Neither word is attested in the Old Persian corpus: Kent's lexicon (KNT.txt) has no gratha and no gravatha, and Bartholomae has no Avestan match either — both are starred reconstructions, and Nourai prints them without the asterisk. (i) *graθa- 'knot' is Hübschmann's: Persische Studien p.93 'Hierher nach Fr. Müller, WZKM. 8, 189 np. girih ‚Knoten“ = ap. *graθa- zu skr. grath ‚verknüpfen“', repeated on p.204 in the chapter on OP θ > NP h ('girih ‚Knoten“ = ap. *graθa- (oben p. 93)'); Mo'in copied it into the Borhān footnote Nourai cites. Modern reconstruction is the same shape but Proto-Iranian rather than Old Persian: Cheung 2007 p.123 *graθH 'to tie (a knot)', Wiktionary Proto-Iranian *graθH- < Proto-Indo-Iranian *grantH-, the -n- of Skt. granth- being the nasal infix that Iranian lost. (ii) 'gravatha' is a misprint. Mo'in's note 4 on Borhān p.1803 reads 'ایرانی باستان *gravathva «نیبرگ ص ۸۴»' — *gravath-va, with a final -va that Nourai's form drops (Dehkhoda quotes the same footnote as 'ایرانی باستان، ظاهراً گروثوه'). Mo'in also calls it Old Iranian, not Old Persian, and prefixes it with 'ظاهراً' ('apparently'), so it is a guess even in the source. The book page (image at data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/173.png) does print 'gravatha', so the extraction is faithful. Finally, the two words do not belong in one box: *graθa- is the etymon of گره and *gravathva that of گروه, and no source derives the second from the first.
nodes.derivation_fa: هیچ‌یک از این دو صورت در کتیبه‌های پارسی باستان گواهی نشده است (در واژه‌نامهٔ کنت نیست) و هر دو بازساخته‌اند؛ نورایی ستارهٔ بازساخت را نیاورده است. صورت *graθa- «گره» از هوبشمان (مطالعات فارسی، ص ۹۳) است که معین در حاشیهٔ برهان قاطع نقل کرده؛ بازساخت امروزین همین صورت است ولی به‌نام «ایرانی آغازین»: چونگ *graθH «گره زدن». اما gravatha خطای چاپی کتاب است: حاشیهٔ ۴ برهان قاطع ص ۱۸۰۳ می‌نویسد «ایرانی باستان *gravathva (نیبرگ ص ۸۴)»، یعنی با پایانهٔ -va که در کتاب افتاده است؛ افزون بر آن معین آن را «ایرانی باستان» و با قید «ظاهراً» آورده، نه پارسی باستان. تصویر صفحهٔ ۱۴۳ کتاب نشان می‌دهد که خوانش اسکن درست است و خطا از خودِ کتاب است.
nodes.book_prints: gratha : knot, tie / gravatha : assemblage, group
nodes.correct_form: Old Iranian *graθa- (Proto-Iranian *graθH-) 'knot'; Old Iranian *gravathva 'group' (Mo'in, after Nyberg p.84)

ref_check.note: The page is right (running head «گره»; printed 1803 = pdf page 600 of BQT_v3_picofile.pdf, NOT pdf 598 as the offset table suggests — the running heads read 1801/1802/1803/1804 on pdf 598/599/600/601; transcription saved to data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BQT/1803.vision.txt). Footnote 10 supports the first word exactly: 'پهلوی grah «تاوادیا ص ۱۶۱» ... از پارسی باستان *gratha ، سانسکریت grath (بستن) «هوبشمان ص۹۳»'. Footnote 4 differs from Nourai on the second: 'پهلوی grôh (دسته، گروه) ... ایرانی باستان *gravathva «نیبرگ ص ۸۴»' — *gravathva, and Old Iranian, not Old Persian.

consulted.note: p.93: 'Hierher nach Fr. Müller, WZKM. 8, 189 np. girih ‚Knoten“ = ap. *graθa- zu skr. grath ‚verknüpfen“' (HUB.txt line 3298); p.204, in the list of OP θ that give NP h: 'girih ‚Knoten“ = ap. *graθa- (oben p. 93)' (line 7233). This is the actual origin of Nourai's box.
grep of KNT.txt for 'grath' returns 0 hits: neither gratha nor gravatha is attested in the Achaemenid inscriptions, so 'Old Persian' can only mean 'reconstructed Old Iranian'.

gives the same consonant skeleton but as a Proto-Iranian verbal root: '*graθH ‚to tie (a knot)” — MIDDLE PERSIAN: BMP glyh /grih/ ‚knot”; PARTHIAN: gryh ‚knot”; KHOTANESE: OKh. grantha-, LKh. gratha- ‚knot”; SOGDIAN: BSogd. γrʾans ‚knot, bond”; NP girih'. No *gravathva anywhere.
no Avestan granθ-/graθa- entry found (grep for 'grantha', 'granθ' returns nothing), i.e. the Old Iranian form has no Avestan witness.

nodes.derivation: گره gereh (classical girih) 'knot' goes back to Middle Persian grih, written glyh in Book Pahlavi: MacKenzie's dictionary has 'grih [glyh | N girih] knot' and Nyberg's glossary the by-form 'grah [glwh]'. The Old Iranian antecedent is *graθa-/*graθH- (Hübschmann p.93; Cheung 2007: 123), with the regular western Iranian development θ > h between the Old and Middle periods — Hübschmann treats girih on p.204 as one of his standard examples of that change (beside rāh < *raθa-, šāh < xšāyaθiya-, چاه < *čāθ-). The a of *graθa- is raised and an anaptyctic vowel breaks the initial cluster gr- > gi-/ge-, giving MP grih [gi'rih] > NP girih, modern Tehran gereh; cognates are Parthian gryh, Sogdian γrʾans, Khotanese grantha-, Kurdish girê, Balochi garanc. Nourai's Persian script and gloss are both right.
nodes.derivation_fa: «گره» از فارسی میانهٔ grih (به خط پهلوی glyh) است؛ مکنزی می‌آورد: 'grih [glyh | N girih] knot'. صورت ایرانی باستان آن *graθa- (چونگ: *graθH) است و تبدیل ث ایرانی باستان به هٔ فارسی همان دگرگونی آوایی است که در راه (*raθa-)، شاه (xšāyaθiya-) و چاه دیده می‌شود — هوبشمان در ص ۲۰۴ همین واژه را نمونهٔ این قاعده آورده است. خوشهٔ آغازین gr- با مصوت میانجی شکسته و girih > گِرِه شده است. همریشه‌ها: پارتی gryh، سغدی γrʾans، کردی girê. ادعای نورایی درست است.

ref_check.note: Borhān p.1803 (pdf 600), headword 'گره ... معروفست اعم ازینکه در ریسمان یا درخت و امثال آن ... و بعربی عقده گویند' with Mo'in's note 10 'پهلوی grah ... از پارسی باستان *gratha ، سانسکریت grath (بستن) «هوبشمان ص۹۳»'.

The six-volume Farhang-e Farsi is not online, so the page number could not be checked; the entry itself is on vajehyab/abadis and reads 'گره (گِ رَ یا رِ) [په .] (اِ.) ۱ - پیچیدگی و درهم شدگی نخ و ریسمان ...' — the tag [په.] = Pahlavi is Mo'in's own statement of the origin Nourai draws.

consulted.note: 'grih [glyh | N girih] knot' (PHD_mackenzie.txt line 2579) — the Middle Persian link that the chart leaves out between the Old Iranian etymon and New Persian.

Nyberg reads the same Book-Pahlavi spelling as 'grah [glwh] troop, company ... NP guroh' for the group-word; for the knot-word his transliteration convention differs, but Mo'in's footnote 10 cites Tavadia p.161 for Pahlavi grah 'knot'.

Horn has no independent article on girih; he only mentions it as the gloss of an Avestan word: 'piyak ‚Knoten“ in aʹpiŷak (vd. 9 (41)). aw. piŷa- ‚Knoten“ ... Vielleicht nur umschreibend (glossirt durch g(i)ris, np. girih)' (HRN.txt line 10915) — confirms the word and its meaning, not the etymology.
lists 'NP girih' among the New West Iranian continuants of *graθH beside 'BMP glyh /grih/', i.e. the same chain Nourai draws.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian grōh 'group, crowd' is solid: MacKenzie 'grōh [glwh | N gurōh] group, crowd', Nyberg's glossary 'grah [glwh] troop, company, with the indef. art. ~-ē ... NP guroh'. What is only 'plausible' is the arrow: Nourai takes grōh out of the same Old Persian box as *graθa- 'knot', but no source derives the group-word from the knot-word. Mo'in, whose footnote is Nourai's ultimate source, gives them separate etymologies on the same page — note 10 'از پارسی باستان *gratha' for گره, note 4 'ایرانی باستان *gravathva «نیبرگ ص ۸۴»' for گروه — and hedges the second with 'ظاهراً'. Cheung's *graθH entry lists no grōh. The semantic step 'tie, bind' → 'band, troop' is of course natural (compare It. gruppo 'knot' → 'group' in the other half of this very chart, and English band), and Wiktionary states it — 'Inherited from Middle Persian glwhʾ /grōh/, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ger- ‚to twist, wind (into a mass)” and cognate with گره' — but its footnote for that claim is Nourai's own book (Ger 1, p.143), so it is not independent evidence.
nodes.derivation_fa: فارسی میانهٔ grōh «دسته، گروه» قطعی است: مکنزی 'grōh [glwh | N gurōh] group, crowd' و نیبرگ 'grah [glwh] troop, company ... NP guroh'. اما پیکانی که نورایی از خانهٔ *gratha «گره» به این خانه می‌کشد پشتیبانی مستقیم ندارد: معین در همان صفحه دو ریشهٔ جداگانه می‌آورد و برای گروه می‌نویسد «ایرانی باستان، ظاهراً *gravathva». تحول معنایی «بستن/گره» به «دسته، جمعیت» طبیعی است (همان‌گونه که gruppo ایتالیایی از «گره» به «group» رسیده) و ویکی‌واژه نیز همین را می‌گوید، اما مأخذِ ویکی‌واژه در همین ماده خودِ کتاب نورایی (ص ۱۴۳) است و استدلال دوری پدید می‌آورد. پس: با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

consulted.note: 'grah [glwh] troop, company, with the indef. art. ~-ē [~+1] 84. - = Paz.; NP guroh' (NYB_vol2_glossary.txt line 1719) — the word, its Book-Pahlavi spelling and the New Persian outcome, but no Old Iranian etymon.

'پهلوی grôh (دسته، گروه)، ارمنی groh (ملت، جمعیت)، بلوچی grôf، ایرانی باستان *gravathva «نیبرگ ص ۸۴»، کردی kuruh' — supports the Pahlavi form and an Old Iranian etymon, but a different one from the knot-word.
the Proto-Iranian knot-root article lists MP grih, Parthian gryh, Sogdian γrʾans and NP girih but no grōh/guroh, i.e. Cheung does not connect the group-word with it.

nodes.derivation: گروه, classical gurōh, modern Iranian goruh 'group, company', is the straightforward continuation of Middle Persian grōh [glwh]: the Pahlavi initial cluster gr- takes the usual anaptyctic u (grōh > gurōh), and Middle Persian long ō survives as ō in Dari and Tajik (gurōh, گوروه/гурӣҳ) but is raised to ū in Iranian Persian (goruh), the same ō > ū raising as in شیر / خون or MP rōz > Ir. Pers. ruz. Mo'in tags the word [په.] 'Pahlavi', Borhān's own note 4 gives 'پهلوی grôh', and it is attested from the earliest New Persian (Ferdowsi, and Rūmi's 'ما نه زان پیلان گولیم ای گروه'), with the loan-descendants Chagatai/Uzbek guruh. Nourai's transliteration 'gorŭh' with the breve is his notation for that raised vowel; script and gloss are right.
nodes.derivation_fa: «گروه» دنبالهٔ مستقیم فارسی میانهٔ grōh است: خوشهٔ آغازین gr- با مصوت میانجی u شکسته و gurōh شده، و واو مجهول (ō) که در دری و تاجیکی مانده، در فارسی ایران به واو معروف (ū) بدل شده است — همان دگرگونی که rōz > روز دارد. معین آن را با نشانهٔ [په.] یعنی پهلوی می‌آورد و حاشیهٔ برهان قاطع نیز «پهلوی grôh». واژه از کهن‌ترین متون فارسی (فردوسی، مولوی) گواهی دارد. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: The word behind French groupe is Italian gruppo 'knot, cluster, group', not grappo. Watkins, the reference Nourai cites, prints it under ger-2 II.4: 'Italian gruppo, an assemblage: GROUP' — 'an assemblage' is verbatim Nourai's gloss, so the box is a copy of that line with the vowel misprinted. Klein: 'group, n. — F. groupe, fr. It. gruppo, ‚group‘, orig. ‚cluster, packet, knot‘, fr. OProvenç. grop, ‚knot‘, which derives fr. Teut. *kruppa, ‚a rounded lump or mass‘'; Webster: 'group, n. [Fr. groupe; It. gruppo, a knot, lump, group; of Germanic origin; compare G. kropf]'; Buck 13.192: 'NE group (fr. Fr. groupe, fr. Ital. gruppo : groppo ‚knot‘)'. Italian grappo does exist — it means 'bunch (of grapes)', synonym of grappolo/graspo, and belongs with Watkins's item I.1e 'Italian dialectal grappa, vine stem' — but it is not the source of groupe and does not mean 'assemblage'. A second, substantive point: the arrow is drawn straight from the Indo-European root to Italian, whereas gruppo is a Germanic loan in Romance (Vulgar Latin *cruppus ← Proto-Germanic *kruppaz 'round mass'), so it reaches the root only through Germanic — the same *kr- family as crop in node #12. The printed page (BOOK/173.png) really does read 'grappo', so this is the book's error, not the extraction's.

nodes.derivation: English group is attested from the 1690s and was, as Buck notes, first an art-critical term — 'assemblage of figures or objects forming a harmonious whole in a painting or design' — taken from French groupe; the general sense 'any assemblage, a number of individuals related in some way' follows by 1736, the verb by 1718. Because the borrowing is post-Great-Vowel-Shift, -ou- is pronounced in the French way (/gruːp/) rather than as in house. Klein, Webster, Buck and Etymonline all give the same three-step chain It. gruppo > F. groupe > E. group, which is Nourai's chain.

nodes.derivation: The gloss is copied word for word from Watkins ('Germanic *krāppōn-, a hook, especially one used in harvesting grapes'), but the form is printed with g-, which no Germanic form of this root can have: PIE *g- gives Germanic *k- by Grimm's law, which is precisely why this whole family appears in English with kr-/cr- (creep, crop, crutch) while its Romance borrowings keep gr-. The attested cognates are Middle Dutch crappe, Old High German krapfo 'hook', Modern German Krapfen, Old Norse krappr; Pokorny sets them up as extension 3.d 'grep- or g(e)rəp-' of ger-3 (Middle Low German krappe 'hook, claw'). Etymonline: grape 'from a Frankish or other Germanic word, from Proto-Germanic *krappon ‚hook”'; Webster: '[OFr. grape, grappe ... from O.H.G. chrapho, a hook]'. So the entry should read Germanic (Frankish) *krāppōn-. The book page prints 'grâppon', so the extraction is faithful and the error is Nourai's — apparently a silent normalisation of the initial to the g- of his root name 'Ger'.
nodes.derivation_fa: معنای این خانه عیناً از واتکینز گرفته شده ('Germanic *krāppōn-, a hook, especially one used in harvesting grapes')، اما صورت با g چاپ شده است و این در ژرمنی ممکن نیست: بر پایهٔ قانون گریم، *g هندواروپایی در ژرمنی به k بدل می‌شود — به همین سبب این خانواده در انگلیسی با cr- پدیدار می‌شود (creep، crop، crutch) و فقط وام‌واژه‌های رمانسی gr- دارند. صورت‌های گواهی‌شده: هلندی میانه crappe، آلمانی علیای کهن krapfo «قلاب»، نوروژی کهن krappr. خطا از خود کتاب است، نه از خوانش اسکن.

'grape, n. — OF. grape, grappe ... fr. OF. craper, graper, ‚to seize with a hook; to gather grapes‘, which is of Teut. origin. Cp. MDu. crappe, OHG. krapfo, ‚a hook‘, G. Krapfen ...'

nodes.derivation: English grape (mid-13c.) is not a direct Germanic inheritance but comes through French: Old French grape/grappe 'hook; bunch of grapes' is a back-formation from graper 'to seize with a hook, gather grapes', itself from the Frankish *krāppōn- of the parent box; the notion is the vine-hook used at the vintage, and the borrowed word displaced native Old English winberige 'wine-berry' (the vine not being grown in England). Watkins states the same route ('Old French graper, to harvest grapes, hence (back-formation) grape, vine, grape: GRAPE'), as do Klein, Webster and Etymonline; Spanish grapa and Italian grappa 'hook' are parallel borrowings of the same Germanic word. The chart's single arrow Germanic → English is thus right in substance but silently omits the Old French stage, which is where the sense 'grape' (rather than 'hook') arose.

nodes.derivation: An empty pass-through box: Nourai uses it to collect the native English words of the root, whose common ancestor is not one Old English word but the whole set of Old English kr-/cr- formations Watkins lists under ger-2 — crypel, crēopan, crycc, cranc-(stæf), cruma, cropp, cribb, cradol, cræt. Labelling that set 'Old English' is legitimate: every one of them is attested in Old English, and the initial cr- is the regular Germanic outcome of PIE *gr- (Grimm's law), which is what makes the box the Germanic-inherited counterpart to the Romance-borrowed Italian/French branch above it.

nodes.derivation: All nine are Watkins's own English outcomes of ger-2 and each has the Old English etymon the parent box implies: cripple < OE crypel (Pok. 'Old English crēper cripple' under greu-b-); creep < OE crēopan (Gmc *kreupan, Pok. greu-b- 'Old Norse krjúpa, Old English creopan ‚creep“'); crutch < OE crycc '(bent) staff' (Pok. greu-g- 'Old English crycce, nengl. crutch', a 'staff with crooked handle'); crank < OE cranc-(stæf) 'weaving implement' (Pok. 'Old English cranc-stæf ‚a weaver's device“'); crumb < OE cruma 'fragment' (Pok. B. gr-eu- 'Old English cruma ‚crumb“, what one scratches from the hard crust'); crop < OE cropp 'cluster, bunch, ear of corn' (Pok. greu-b- 'Old English cropp ‚bundle of berries or flowers, ear, goiter, crop“'); crib < OE cribb 'manger' (Pok. ger-bʰ- 'Old English cribb ‚crib, manger“'); cradle < OE cradol (Pok. *gr-et(h)- '*kradula- ‚the plaited“'). The one that needs a footnote is cart: Watkins writes 'Old English cræt and Old Norse kartr, wagon: CART', but the actual Middle English carte is generally taken from the Norse word — Etymonline, 'c. 1200 ... from Old Norse kartr or a similar Scandinavian source, akin to and replacing Old English cræt' — so its parent box would more accurately be Old Norse. The semantics throughout are the root's two halves: 'bent/hooked' (cripple, creep, crutch, crank) and 'rounded mass / plaited container' (crumb, crop, crib, cradle, cart).

nodes.derivation: Nourai's own note is the correction: the form is Middle Dutch, not modern Dutch (modern Dutch is krul). Middle Dutch crulle/crul 'curly' is item I.16 of Watkins's ger-2 ('Middle Dutch crulle, curly: CRULLER, CURL'), and Pokorny puts the family under the s-extension greu-s- on p.389: 'Old High German Middle High German krol(-ll-) ‚frizzy“ (*kruzla-). Middle High German krol(le), krulle ‚curl“, Norwegian krull'. Proto-Germanic *kruzlō̄ gives Middle Dutch crulle by the regular West Germanic rhotacism-plus-assimilation zl > ll, and the whole set (MDu. crul, MHG krolle, Norw. krull, Dan. krølle) belongs together. The book's own NOTE that this is a Middle Dutch word is right and should be kept.

nodes.derivation: The English word is certainly this family, and the mechanism is the striking one: metathesis of r and the vowel. Middle English crul(le) 'curly' and the verb crullen were re-ordered to curl(en) in the 14th-15th c. — Klein: 'curl, tr. and intr. v. — ME. curlen, metathesized fr. ME. crullen, fr. crul, ‚curly‘ ... For the metathesis of ME. crullen to curlen cp. curd'; the same shift produced curd from crud and, later, bird from brid. What is only 'plausible' is the arrow as drawn, Middle Dutch → English: Klein says ME crul is 'related to' MDu. crulle rather than taken from it, and Wiktionary writes 'From metathesis of Middle English crulle ‚curled, curly“, of uncertain origin but probably from an unrecorded Old English word or from Middle Dutch crul, crulle', ultimately Proto-Germanic *kruzlō̄. So the word may be native English rather than a Dutch loan; either way it goes back to the same Germanic *kruzl-, and Watkins's ger-2 I.16 files CURL under Middle Dutch crulle exactly as Nourai does.
